Heisenberg group · sub-Laplacian wave equation

Listening to the Heisenberg wave

A point source at the origin is struck once. Seven observers, all at sub-Riemannian distance 1 from it and differing only in the ratio \(\theta=t/|z|^2\), record the displacement as the wave passes. Each click is one geodesic from the source to the observer. The same observers are listening points on the wave kernel page, where their clicks play in step with the animation.

level−72 dB … 0 dB

What you are hearing

The medium obeys \(\partial_s^2u+\mathcal Lu=0\) on \(\mathbb H^1\), with \(u(0)=0\) and \(\partial_su(0)=\delta_0\), so the recorded signal is \(u(s,p)=\mathcal L^{-1/2}\sin(s\sqrt{\mathcal L})\,\delta_0(p)\). The dilation law \(u(rs,\delta_rp)=r^{-3}u(s,p)\) means that standing nearer the source only plays the same recording faster and louder: what the sound is like depends only on \(\theta\). Every observer here is at distance 1, and the pacing decides how many seconds of audio that distance takes.

Below the first threshold \(\theta\approx1.123\) a single geodesic joins the source to the observer, so there is one click. Each later threshold adds a pair of geodesics that have passed a conjugate point. Their clicks cycle through four shapes: a click, a two-sided snap (the Hilbert transform of a click), a click of reversed sign, and a reversed snap. After the last geodesic has arrived the signal does not fall silent: a tail remains, so the sharp Huygens principle fails. Measured 0.1 s after the last click in the fast clips, the tail is about 83 dB below the peak in the horizontal plane, 59 dB at \(\theta=0.6\), 39 dB at \(\theta=10.2\) and 24 dB at \(\theta=47.9\). Only the last two are clearly audible. The click peaks scale with the bandwidth and the tail does not, so a duller microphone would hear relatively more tail.

On the axis through the source the geodesics of length \(\sqrt{4\pi m|t|}\) return after \(m\) loops, for every \(m\ge1\), and the signal is exactly

\[u(s,(0,t))=\sum_{m\ge1}(-1)^m\,m\,\big(s^2-4\pi m|t|\big)_+^{-3/2}\qquad\text{(finite part).}\]

With arrival time \(T\), click \(m\) comes at \(T\sqrt m\), so at time \(\tau\) the clicks come at a rate of \(2\tau/T^2\) per second. Their signs alternate, so only odd harmonics of \(\tau/T^2\) Hz are present: a buzz whose pitch rises steadily, about 200 Hz at the end of the fast clip. The clicks also grow slowly, roughly like \(m^{1/4}\), because each return is focused.

How it is computed

Mehler's formula writes the heat kernel as an integral over \(y\) of \(\frac{y}{2\sinh y}e^{-\varphi(y)/4\tau}\), with \(\varphi(y)=|z|^2\,y\coth y+4ity\). Inverting the transform that links \(e^{-\tau\mathcal L}\) to \(\cos(s\sqrt{\mathcal L})\) gives, along any contour on which \(\varphi\) is real,

\[u(s,p)=-\frac1{\pi^2}\ \mathrm{f.p.}\!\int_\Gamma\frac{y}{2\sinh y}\,\big(s^2-\varphi(y)\big)_+^{-3/2}\,dy .\]

For \(t>0\) the real line is pushed down. The saddle points of \(\varphi\) are \(y=-i\psi\) with \(\frac{2\psi-\sin2\psi}{8\sin^2\psi}=\theta\), and \(\varphi(-i\psi)\) is the squared length of a geodesic. The deformed contour is a loop around \(-i\pi m\) for each pair of geodesics that exists, plus one curve to infinity; each saddle point on it gives one click. The page's audio traces these curves numerically and evaluates the integral, smoothed in time by a Gaussian that halves the amplitude at 8 kHz. That smoothing equals applying \(e^{-\varepsilon\mathcal L}\) to the source, with \(\varepsilon=\sigma^2/2\). The source code and a full account are in src/heisenberg_audio.py and the README.

Checks

At a lower bandwidth (\(\varepsilon=2\times10^{-3}\)) the signal for every observer was compared with a direct sum over Landau levels. On a grid of spacing \(\sigma/40\) the largest difference is \(1.1\times10^{-3}\) of that observer's peak. On the grid used for the audio, which has the same ratio \(\sigma/10.3\), it is \(9.8\times10^{-3}\). These are sampled numerical checks, not error bounds.
